posts.cooked:
Honestly I'm not too impressed.  I like Setback, his "just, y'know" attitude is very fitting, I've been thinking that the missing archetype for the game was of a roguish, underwhelming kind of hero, not quite a mercenary (since those have professional pride to consider) but someone who's pretty much entirely selfish and shallow and generally "of the world" (which implies something very different than "worldly").  The Naturalist will probably be fun to play, although his Nature-vs.-corporations flavor is Anvilicious in the extreme.  But the others really don't do it for me.  "Parse" makes no sense whatsoever to me, seems to have been inserted as a pander to people who want to see a "disabled" hero...and did Miss Information really need to have a nemesis?  I interpreted the brackets symbol as connoting a LACK of nemesis (and if she has a nemesis at all, shouldn't it be the entire Freedom Five?).

Likewise, I have several problems with The Sentinels, starting with their name being more than a little confusing when it's also the name of the game.  The fact that Medico is gay again seems like it's being done as "props" to a fringe group, and completely unnecessary since we already have a homosexual hero; then there's also the fact that we were told there would never be a healer (having a "hero" who is 1/4 a healer is a novel solution to that issue, but I'm deeply puzzled as to how this is going to work).  Plus, personally, the whole "Idealist is mentally a child" thing REALLY squicks me, and finally there seems to be a continuity error with Writhe, as he's described being stopped by the existing three Sentinels, but we saw him on one of Tachyon's cards and her role wasn't mentioned.  So if he's a hero now, why is Tachyon fighting him?  (For that matter, why is Expatriette shooting Setback on Shock Rounds?)  Ultimately, I'm baffled by the idea we're getting EIGHT new heroes instead of five, when we already have a single Villain deck that represents five actual Villains; it seems like this is going to get cluttered (and just imagine Sentinels and four other heroes vs. the Ennead! how would you ever find enough table space?).

Alone of the new characters, I have no real opinion on KNYFE, past that I lack the patience to type her name with periods.  "Short-range energy bursts" seems like kind of a lame power, but a hero with a connection to The Block seems like a vaguely neat concept (although it makes me think some of the Agents should have had a nemesis icon for her).  Past that, my assessment of her is pretty much "eh".  So, liking Mainstay, a little fond of Naturalist, neutral on KNYFE, a little down on the Sentinels, and very unimpressed with Parse.  (All this is of course a very ignorant prejudgment which will have nothing to do with how they play.)

I'm going to put this out there briefly and then try to get the thread relatively back on topic, as this is a board about superhero card games, not LGBT representation.  There are plenty of LGBT people in the world; I am proud to be one.  There are plenty of black, Hispanic, Asian, what-have-you people as well.  The comic book industry (and the archetypes that they ape) often strays way too far towards catering to the tastes of straight, white, middle-class men.  Any inclusion of characters that are not straight, white men is all right by me, because it's a step towards realism.  It's not pandering to have strong empowered heroes.  It's not pandering to include developed, nuanced characters who deal with their ethnicity or their sexuality in a mature manner.   And, above all else, >G have done a pretty solid job in diversifying a notoriously non-diverse segment of entertainment.

 

Now, back to real discussion!

I said:

  • Some type of Hawkeye/Green Arrow archer character.

Well, Parse definitely fits that mold.  I like the idea of a data analyst/hacker opposing the "bureaucratic" villain of Miss Information, but the Archery theme seems a little light on her.   Obviously I haven't seen the cards--I'm not a playtester--but when I picture Green Arrow or Hawkeye, I picture lots of gimmick arrows:  line arrows, explosive-tipped arrows, sonic stunner arrows, etc.  I'm kind of ambivalent about Parse's costume, though I do like the archery gauntlets, which look like she stole them from Hawkeye, as drawn by David Aja.

I said:

  • Some type of shapeshifty Beast Boy-type character.

Hit the nail on the head with this one!  The Naturalist certainly fits this mold perfectly.  I'm not sure what to think of his links to Akash'Bhuta and Argent Adept, but it feels like his background apes that of Black Panther or Moon Knight, which I like.  I'm interested to see what each of his forms will bring.  I'd assume that Rhinoceros and Crocodile are both forms, as they're mentioned directly in the text, though I'd like to see what else is in that deck.  Perhaps a constrictor-snake form to immobilize a villain target and keep them from dealing damage?  A bird-type card could scout the Environment or Villain decks, perhaps?  Lots of options here.

I said: 

  • "Twitchy", with some kind of probability control (he'll have the dice icon as his)

Got this one, too!  While I didn't bank on Setback having so many links to Baron Blade (apparently trying to create his own Legacy-type character), a bad-luck controlling character seems pretty awesome.  My wife once played an ICONS game as a bad-luck controller named Murphy...it was a blast!

  • A size-changing female Thorathian, a la Giganta.

Wow, was I ever off.  I didn't see this one coming at all, though having an actual FILTER agent (even a former one) as a hero makes sense.  KNYFE feels a lot like a mash-up of Black Widow and Psylocke to me, both of which are characters that don't get their due in the comics world.  Plus, I love the idea of a female character being a strong, melee bruiser:  it's just not something that you see often enough.  I wonder if the >G gang has been reading Deconnick's run on Captain Marvel, mayhaps?

I said:

Ooh, I forgot about biker guy!

I'm betting he'll be Mainstay--the enigmatic 5th from my list above.  I'd put money on him being a Lobo/Ghost Rider type dude--lots of chains, hooks, and knives, with some type of motorcycle or other vehicle, which could be represented like Turret Mode or Pushing the Limits.  I'd also bank on him having a lot of one-shots, instead of ongoings.

When crafting the bios for SotM characters, any information about their backstory/personal life/etc that "makes the cut" is something that we consider important for the reader to know or understand in order to get a good sense of and feeling for the personality and motivations of the character. However, there are many details about every character that are True, and Canon, but have never yet been revealed. This is either because we are saving the information for a more opportune time, or because it is just not important enough to have come up yet, but may in the future.

Tachyon's sexual orientation is a good example of this phenomenon. Her internal back story had always included her relationship status and sexual orientation, but it happened to not come up until the Freedom Four Annual #1, when there was a plot reason to include some home life scenes from various characters. For Legacy, by contrast, we felt that his relationship status and sexual orientation was more important to understanding his character, so it is alluded to more prominently.

Rest assured, there are a ton of currently unrevealed details about all aspects of all of the characters, from personality traits to disabilities to ethnic backgrounds to preferences of all sorts. Hopefully we'll have the opportunity to eventually share them!

Christopher and his crew have gone the extra mile in terms of worldbuilding by making heroes that didn't exist before 2010 or so feel as rich and storied as characters that have been in existence since the 1960s (or long before!).  Part of doing such means doing careful, nuanced characterization.  And, whether you like it or not, that means attaching history and backstory to each character that makes them feel like a fully-developed character.  "Tactfully avoiding" the issue of a hero's sexuality isn't a mature attitude to take, as it leaves out an entire important facet of character.  When you're building a whole Multiverse, you have to consider these characters as whole people.

Let's take, for example, Young Legacy.  There's nothing that's been stated about her sexuality so far, but the inclusion of a dynamic as nuanced as sexual preference provides a platform for character development.  What happens if Young Legacy is a lesbian?  Her powers are passed on by genetics.  Would she be willing to end the Legacy line to live an honest, free life?  I'm not saying that this is the direction that >G should go, but rather it's an entire plot-line of possibility that could not potentially exist without open, frank discussion of sexuality.

I'm going to call a spade a spade here and say outright that your viewpoints on what "should be" and "should not be" acceptable in an LGBT character is homophobic, wrong-headed, and backwards.  Your examples rely on overblown, misrepresented stereotypes (Argent Adept as the unmanly bard, playing a "girl's" instrument, the flute; Char and Mainstay as burly bears) and your statements bely fear of the unknown:  the "hidden" homosexual, out to ruin, to jump out and corrupt, malign, and seduce.  That's pure, unmitigated homophobia.

You sought to raise my own preferences briefly after I mentioned that I'm both bisexual and I have a wife.  Both statements are correct:  I am a bisexual man married to a wonderful woman (who also happens to be bisexual/bi-curious).  Believe it or not–whether you'd like to admit it or not–I'm one of thousands in that situation:  a bisexual in a long-term relationship that appears, to all outside appearances, to be straight.  I'm also a high school teacher, a published writer and game designer, a fan of Pittsburgh Steelers football, a comic book nerd, and pretty reasonable cook.  All of these are a part of me, yet none specifically define me.  I am, as you are, a sum of my experiences.  Further, I (and pretty much every other member of the LGBT community) don't adhere to a series of outdated, homophobic stereotypes.  My sexuality is a part of who I am, but it is not what defines me.  And you certainly wouldn't be able to tell that I'm bisexual by passing me on the street; I'm no stereotype.

You know what would be gratuitious and unnecessary in SotM?  If the creators chose to make their gay character "Queer-Mo":  a burly man in a leather harness and pink tutu who flings razor-sharp pink triangles at his foes.  The stereotypes that you're specifically choosing to (wrongfully) uphold are absurd and overblown.  No LGBT person wants this as a superhero.  No person wants this as a superhero.  Rather, I (and I think pretty much anyone, really) would much prefer a mature, reasonable take on a hero's personality–if that take includes their sexuality as a part of them, so be it.  

The fact that >G has taken up that viewpoint and dealt with it with maturity–Tachyon's sexuaility is a part of her, not what defines her; same with Medico–makes me proud, as it epitomizes everything that is right and reasonable about the LGBT rights movement.

Here's another possibility to explore about all of this -- the game started out feeling pretty Silver Age.  The heroes were fresh takes on old tropes, but most were still tropey enough to feel like classic heroes.  This newer batch of heroes feels a bit like comics in the 90s & 2000s to me, where the big comics felt they needed to up the diversity level to keep things fresh.  They tossed in some gay characters, they tossed in some characters whose powers could almost be seen as disabilities (who's that X-man whose power blew off the bottom part of his face?, or that other X-man Maggott whose "power" was that he had a pair of slugs in his stomach), they decided that Ant Man beat his wife, etc.  Some of it worked, some of it didn't, but it was a more-or-less natural evolution of the genre in an attempt to keep up with the world of its readers.

There's rarely a "correct" play/action - there's an answer that might result in more damage or a better tactical position, but often it's more fun to do whatever we feel like doing. One of the keys to a team game is each player gets to make their own decision; the rest of us should contribute information and make sure everyone understands our thoughts and preferences, but in the end that player should make the decision.

For example, when we're doing demos at Cons, I will often point out cards that are useful or appropriate, but if someone says they want Tempest to play Cleansing Downpour as his first turn play (even though he has far better choices), I'll make sure he understands what the other cards actually do then move on - it's that player's choice. They have a lot more fun because they're able to actually make choices and experience the consequences (positive or negative) of that choice.

I've been on both sides of this situation, and in general I've found everyone has a much more enjoyable game when they're allowed to do what they want, even if someone else at the table doesn't agree with it.

I'm with Nielzabub here.

Medico being gay makes him more interesting as a character. I immediately wondered how that had affected his relationship with Mainstay, when did he come out, and how did Mainstay respond initially? It also tells us that Mainstay is accepting of Medico's sexuality at least now since they're still good friends. It tells us that Medico and Caleb as gay males probably had to fight pretty hard to even be allowed to adopt the Idealist and that they likely face continual prejudice on a day-to-day basis - there are many people out there who, while they claim not to have a problem with non-straight couples, insist that children should be brought up only in a traditional one-mum-one-dad family unit. This means that their family relationship is likely very strong in order to have even considered going though the adoption process, and also as a result of the struggles I assume they've had.

This of course impacts the Idealist too - she's much less likely to be pressured into conforming to particular societal expectations, especially gender-based ones. She'll also face prejudice.

If Medico was straight, none of these issues are there. And I believe his sexuality is important enough to be mentioned in his bio since it talks about the adoption, and the gender of his partner is absolutely relevant to that.

As for Parse, sure, the Aspbergers mention feels a little clumsy. But it works within the context of a being-able-to-spot-patterns-that-most-people-can't type character - it's clearly referencing the real-world phenomenon of "savant syndrome" (previously known as idiot savant or autistic savant) in which a person (usually on the autistic spectrum or with severe mental disability) hyper-fixates on a particular narrow area of expertise and subsequently develops an ability in excess of what would be considered "normal". It's a decent reason why Parse has natural "superhuman powers" even before Omniton affected her.

And looking beyond the game here, however bad or good the writing, I for one am extremely happy to see the inclusion of heroes/villains who aren't straight white American males, a group which is traditionally extremely over-represented in the genre. As a non-American not-entirely-straight female with a disability myself, it's refreshing to find a game that essentially gives the message that regardless of gender/colour/sexuality/nationality/age or even species, or even biology, all these people are worthy of being proper characters.
